title: Generics
subtitle: Type parameters, constraints, keyof, inference, erasure

cards.front: What are generics?
cards.meaning: They parameterize types the way functions parameterize values. You write one implementation; each call site keeps specific type information instead of collapsing to any or duplicating overloads.

cards.front: Generics vs any vs overloads — why generics exist?
cards.meaning: Without generics you either use any and lose safety downstream, or copy-paste/overload per type, which does not scale. Generics keep one implementation and preserve the relationship (element type in ⇒ same type out) per call.

cards.front: What does firstElement<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined preserve?
cards.meaning: T is inferred from the argument: [1, 2, 3] gives number | undefined; ['a', 'b'] gives string | undefined. The function is shared; the input–output element relationship is preserved per call.

cards.front: How is T usually inferred on identity<T>(x: T): T?
cards.meaning: Inference usually comes from arguments. identity(1) infers T as 1 or number depending on context; identity<string>('a') passes T explicitly. Return type is often inferred too; annotate when it clarifies.

cards.front: Why would a generic have two type parameters?
cards.meaning: To keep two independent relationships. mapPair<A, B>(a: A, b: B): [A, B] preserves each argument’s type in the tuple instead of collapsing both to one T or any.
cards.example: function mapPair<A, B>(a: A, b: B): [A, B] { return [a, b]; }

cards.front: When do you pass explicit type arguments like fn<User>(…)?
cards.meaning: When inference fails: no arguments to infer from (identity() needs <T> or a default), conflicting inferences from multiple args, or too-wide contextual types. Then pass explicit type arguments.

cards.front: What is ApiResponse<T> — a factory or a value?
cards.meaning: A generic type alias is a factory for concrete types. Instantiating ApiResponse<User> fixes data: User and status: number. Generic types are not runtime values.

cards.front: What does interface Repository<T, ID> parameterize?
cards.meaning: The entity type T and the id type ID: findById(id: ID): Promise<T | null> and save(entity: T): Promise<T>. Instantiating Repository<User, string> fixes both parameters.

cards.front: Can classes be generic?
cards.meaning: Yes. class Box<T> { constructor(public value: T) {} } is a generic class; each instance carries a concrete T for value.

cards.front: What does T extends { name: string } do?
cards.meaning: It limits what T may be so you can use known properties. x.name is allowed because the constraint guarantees name: string. Without that extends, x.name is an error.
cards.example: function label<T extends { name: string }>(x: T): string { return x.name; }

cards.front: T extends Foo vs annotating the param as Foo — difference?
cards.meaning: T extends Foo means T must be assignable to Foo and can be richer. Returning T keeps the full caller type. Annotating the param as Foo alone would widen and drop extra properties.
cards.example: function withName<T extends { name: string }>(x: T): T { return x; }

cards.front: What does getProp<T, K extends keyof T>(obj, key: K): T[K] buy you?
cards.meaning: Keys are checked and the return type is exact — typos and misuse fail at compile time, unlike (obj: any, key: string): any.

cards.front: keyof T, then K extends keyof T, then T[K] — causal chain?
cards.meaning: keyof T is the union of property names. K extends keyof T allows only those names. T[K] is indexed access: the type of that property. Together they type a safe key accessor.

cards.front: What does type Page<T = unknown> mean when you write Page?
cards.meaning: Default type parameters supply a type when callers omit the argument. Page alone is Page<unknown>; Page<User> is UserPage. Defaults help when a parameter is often a common choice (useState-style APIs, optional config types).

cards.front: Why give createSet a default T = string?
cards.meaning: With no arguments there is nothing to infer from. T = string lets createSet() return Set<string> without an explicit type argument, while callers can still pass T.
cards.example: function createSet<T = string>(): Set<T> { return new Set(); }

cards.front: Can you instanceof T, new T(), or inspect T at runtime?
cards.meaning: No. Generics are erased — T is not a value. You cannot new T(), instanceof T, or inspect T at runtime. That is the same erasure story as other TypeScript types.

cards.front: Why is return {} as T in make<T>(): T a smell?
cards.meaning: There is no runtime T to construct or check. The assertion pretends an empty object is T. Factories that need instances must take a runtime constructor value instead.

cards.front: How do you construct a generic T at runtime?
cards.meaning: Pass a runtime constructor: factory<T>(Ctor: new () => T): T { return new Ctor(); }. The value Ctor exists at runtime; the type parameter T does not.
cards.example: function factory<T>(Ctor: new () => T): T { return new Ctor(); }

cards.front: Why is useAsync generic?
cards.meaning: Success state carries data: T inferred from () => Promise<T>, so on success state.data is User after fetchUser. One hook, correct data type per fetch — a common whiteboard exercise combining generics, discriminated unions, and closures.

cards.front: How is useAsync state modeled?
cards.meaning: A discriminated union: idle | loading | { status: 'success'; data: T } | { status: 'error'; error: unknown }. T only exists on success; error is unknown until narrowed.
cards.example: useState<{ status: 'idle' } | { status: 'loading' } | { status: 'success'; data: T } | { status: 'error'; error: unknown }>({ status: 'idle' })

cards.front: How does inference work on List<T> with renderItem?
cards.meaning: T flows from items: T[] to renderItem: (item: T) => React.ReactNode. Inference links the array element type to the callback parameter without any on renderItem.
cards.example: function List<T>({ items, renderItem }: ListProps<T>) { return <>{items.map(renderItem)}</>; }

cards.front: Why avoid React.FC<Props<T>> for a generic component?
cards.meaning: Writing a generic React component as React.FC<Props<T>> is awkward. Prefer function Comp<T>(props: Props<T>).

cards.front: What is Repository<T, ID> in Nest / TypeORM style?
cards.meaning: One abstraction, many entities: UserRepository implements Repository<User, string> with typed findById and save. Same pattern as TypeORM-style Repository<Entity> — typed IDs and returns without duplicating the interface per entity.

cards.front: Can Nest inject an open generic T?
cards.meaning: No. Runtime DI still needs concrete classes or tokens. Generics do not exist at runtime for Nest to inject “T”. Thinking Nest can inject an open generic without a concrete class is a common mistake.

cards.front: What is the identity / pair generic pattern?
cards.meaning: The interview-toolkit sketch <T>(x: T): T — and pair as mapPair<A, B>. One implementation that returns the same type(s) it received.

cards.front: What is the container generic pattern?
cards.meaning: Wrap a payload in a named shape: ApiResponse<T>, Box<T>. The container fields stay fixed; T is the varying inner type.

cards.front: What is the constrained-field generic pattern?
cards.meaning: <T extends { id: string }>(x: T) — require a known field so the body can use it, while still returning or preserving the richer T.

cards.front: Where does Awaited<T> sit relative to generics?
cards.meaning: Promise unwrap is a utility type (advanced chapter). It is part of the generics interview toolkit as “unwrap a Promise,” not something this unit implements from scratch.

cards.front: Why is using any instead of T a mistake?
cards.meaning: It “makes it compile” but drops the call-site relationship generics exist to preserve. You lose downstream safety — the problem generics were meant to solve.

cards.front: What goes wrong if you over- or under-constrain T?
cards.meaning: Over-constraining breaks inference; under-constraining means you cannot use the properties you need. Prefer the minimal constraint that unlocks those properties.

cards.front: Is T extends any a useful constraint?
cards.meaning: No. It is a pointless constraint. It does not add property knowledge and does not improve inference.

cards.front: Should you force explicit type arguments everywhere?
cards.meaning: No. Inference from arguments usually works. Force <T> when inference fails (no args, conflicts, too-wide context), not as a default style.
